conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode (bear mirror per Brooks). Helpers: overlap(i) = (min(high[i],high[i+1]) - max(low[i],low[i+1])) / range(i) (per V02's convention); avgVolume(n) = plain mean of volume over the n bars ending 1 bar ago (excludes the current, possibly still-forming bar); swingHigh(n)/swingLow(n) = the n-th most recent confirmed swing pivot per T17-01's pivotStrength-bar confirmation; tick = instrument minimum move; trendDurationBars = bars since the always-in/trend direction last flipped (a research-grade concept, see V07-01).

candidates.name: FinalFlagCandidatePrimitive
candidates.quote: The flag occurs in a trend that has gone on for dozens of bars... The flag is mostly horizontal and has signs of strong two-sided trading, such as several trend bars in the opposite direction, bars with prominent tails, several reversals, and bars that overlap the previous bar by at least 50 percent.
candidates.description: Primitive: after a trend has run for at least N bars, a mostly-horizontal pullback/trading range showing signs of strong two-sided trading (high bar-to-bar overlap, several counter-trend bodies, prominent tails, multiple internal reversals) is a final-flag candidate - traded the same way whether or not it later turns out to be the actual last flag. It is usually 5 to 10 bars or more but can be as short as a single bar (any pause bar, including a doji, qualifies as a one-bar final flag).
candidates.pseudocode:
highOverlapBarFraction = countIf(overlap(i) >= overlapThreshold, i in 0..flagBars-1) / flagBars;
isFinalFlagCandidate = trendDurationBars >= minTrendBars && highOverlapBarFraction >= minOverlapFraction && flagBars >= 1
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification used as a precondition for other candidates in this file)

complexity.reason: the bar-overlap counting itself is a simple window loop, but 'a trend that has gone on for dozens of bars' needs a trend-duration measure built on the always-in/trend-direction classification, which MINING.md itself flags as research-grade before it can be coded (a design decision is needed, e.g. a moving-average-slope or higher-high/lower-low run definition)

notes: Brooks explicitly says the final-flag LABEL is retrospective ('every reversal follows some kind of flag'); the operationally testable part is the two-sided-trading shape test, not the 'final' label itself.
'dozens of bars' is read as 30 for minTrendBars; not a number Brooks gives explicitly.

candidates.name: MicroFlagFromFailedMicroTrendLineBreak
candidates.quote: A micro trend line breakout pullback is of a one-bar or micro final flag... If the sell-off fails within a bar or two and then the market reverses back up from a lower low, double bottom, or higher low, this last sell-off is the breakout pullback and the original small breakout becomes the final flag in the micro bear trend.
candidates.description: When a one- or two-bar breakout of a micro trend line fails within a bar or two (price reverses back through the breakout bar's own extreme), the tiny breakout itself is reclassified as a one-bar (or micro) final flag and the failed follow-through becomes a breakout-pullback entry back in the original micro-trend direction.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the failed micro-breakout reversal bar's high

complexity.reason: micro trend-line projection over a very short pivot window plus a fast failure test

notes: Micro trend lines are the Trends-book's micro-channel primitive (Ch.16); this restates its failure case as a final-flag instance.

candidates.name: FailedFinalFlagBecomesBreakoutPullback
candidates.quote: If a final flag reversal triggers but the reversal fails within a couple of bars, this becomes a failed final flag. A failed final flag is a setup for a resumption of the original trend and therefore is a breakout pullback.
candidates.description: If a reversal signal fired off a final-flag candidate (V07-01) but price reverses back through that signal's own stop level within a couple of bars, the final flag has failed: treat the failure as a breakout-pullback entry and resume trading with the original trend rather than the reversal.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the failed reversal's own signal-bar high (or the bar that closes back above it)

complexity.reason: inherits V07-01's research-grade trend/flag detection plus a fast-failure bar-count test on the reversal attempt

candidates.name: SecondEntryAfterFailedFinalFlagReversal
candidates.quote: If the rally goes for only a bar or two and reverses down again, it sets up a second entry short from the original potential final flag. If the reversal succeeds, it is a final flag reversal.
candidates.description: If the breakout-pullback move produced by a failed final-flag reversal (V07-03) itself only lasts a bar or two before reversing back in the ORIGINAL reversal direction, take a second-entry trade in that original (final-flag) reversal direction.
candidates.pseudocode:
breakoutPullbackFailedWithinBars = close[0] < reversalSignalBarLow && (currentBarIndex - pullbackStartIndex) <= secondEntryWindowBars;
enterShortNextBarOpen = breakoutPullbackFailedWithinBars // second attempt at the original short reversal
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop below the second-attempt signal bar's low

complexity.reason: chains V07-01 and V07-03's detections with a further bar-count and failure test

notes: Likely overlaps with the generic 'second entry' counting primitive already mined (SecondEntryPullbackCount V01-05, SecondReversalSignal V02-20); dedup pass should compare.

candidates.name: TwoShrinkingHorizontalFlagsSetUpWedge
candidates.quote: Sometimes there will be two consecutive horizontal flags with the second one being smaller, and the breakout from the second one can lead to a wedge reversal.
candidates.description: When two consecutive horizontal trading-range flags form back to back with the second noticeably smaller (narrower range) than the first, the breakout from the second flag is more likely to set up a wedge-type reversal.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter raising the odds assigned to a subsequent wedge classification)

complexity.reason: 'horizontal flag' and 'smaller' are both undefined; needs a design decision for both the flag-shape test and the size-comparison threshold

candidates.name: SmallFinalFlagAfterClimaxSpikeExpectation
candidates.quote: Sometimes a final flag can be only one or two bars long and develop after a strong spike... The breakout from that small flag often reverses after a bar or two and usually results in a two-legged pullback that lasts for 10 bars or more... frequently is followed by a test of the trend extreme within 10 to 20 bars.
candidates.description: A one- or two-bar pause after a strong multi-bar trend-bar spike (a potential exhaustive climax) is a candidate final flag; if its breakout reverses within a bar or two, expect at least a two-legged pullback of 10 or more bars, though a full trend reversal is not reliable - more often the trend extreme is tested again within 10 to 20 bars.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (sets bar-count expectations for trade management after a climax-spike final flag)

complexity.reason: needs a persistent count of consecutive large trend bars (a spike classifier) plus the final-flag failure test of V07-01/V07-03

notes: Distinct from V05-08/consecutive-climax-correction primitives by giving a specific 10-20 bar re-test window in addition to the usual 2-legs/10-bars pullback figure.

candidates.name: TradingRangeMidpointMagnetPullback
candidates.quote: the result is that there is a magnetic effect in the middle of these trading ranges, and most breakout attempts do not go far before the market is pulled back into the trading range.
candidates.description: Inside a trading range or flag with pronounced two-sided trading, breakout attempts beyond either edge tend to fail and be pulled back toward the range's own midpoint; fade breakouts toward that midpoint rather than expecting them to run.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter / target used by breakout-fade entries and exits)

complexity.reason: depends on classifying 'the market is in a trading range', a design decision MINING.md itself calls out as research-grade

notes: Likely duplicates a trading-range-magnet primitive already mined from the Ranges book (Part II, 'Magnets, Support and Resistance', Chapters 7-10).

candidates.name: FinalFlagReversalStrengthRequiresPriorTrendLineBreak
candidates.quote: The trend reversal is more likely if there was a strong bear leg (a sign of selling pressure) in the flag, or earlier, that broke well below the bull trend line.
candidates.description: A final-flag reversal is more likely to succeed into a genuine trend reversal (rather than just a pullback) if a strong counter-trend leg, either inside the flag itself or earlier in the trend, already broke the prevailing trend line by a clear margin.
candidates.pseudocode:
priorTrendLineBrokenByMargin = trendLineBrokenWithin(lookbackBars) && trendLineBreakMargin[0] >= breakMarginTicks * tick;
reversalMoreLikely = isFinalFlagCandidate && priorTrendLineBrokenByMargin
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter raising confidence in the reversal, not a distinct order)

complexity.reason: needs trend-line projection from pivots and a break-margin test in addition to V07-01's flag detection

notes: Same family as TrendLineBreakBeforeReversal (V01-01) / TrendLineBreakRequiredForReversal (VP1-01), restated for the final-flag context.

candidates.name: VeryLongTrendReversalBecomesFlagNotOppositeTrend
candidates.quote: If the original trend lasted for 50 to 100 bars, then the reversal will more likely evolve into a large flag rather than a trend in the opposite direction.
candidates.description: When the trend preceding a final-flag reversal has lasted 50 to 100 bars or more, temper the reversal's profit expectations: it is more likely to evolve into a large sideways flag than into a genuine trend in the opposite direction.
candidates.pseudocode:
isVeryLongTrend = trendDurationBars >= veryLongTrendBars;
expectLargeFlagInsteadOfOppositeTrend = isFinalFlagCandidate && isVeryLongTrend
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (moderates target/hold-time expectations after the reversal signal)

candidates.name: FlagPullbackExitAtTrendExtremeTest
candidates.quote: With any bull flag, pullback traders buy and look to exit on a test of the trend's extreme (the most recent high). They prefer to take profits above the old high, but watch carefully to see if the market stalls below it.
candidates.description: For a with-trend flag-pullback long entry, take profit at (or just above) a test of the trend's most recent swing extreme; if price stalls just below that extreme instead of clearing it, exit there rather than holding for more.
candidates.pseudocode:
trendExtreme = swingHigh(1);
exitLongAtTarget = high[0] >= trendExtreme - stallTicks * tick
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit at or just below the prior swing high

complexity.reason: the target is a confirmed swing pivot, so it inherits T17-01's pivot-detection mechanics

candidates.name: FlagBreakoutConfirmationRequiresCloseMargin
candidates.quote: when a bull flag breaks out to the downside, traders want to see a strong bear trend bar with a close that is several ticks below the bottom of the flag, like the bear trend bar that formed two bars before bar 13.
candidates.description: A breakout of a flag is only considered confirmed (strong enough to make with-trend traders give up on the flag) when a trend bar CLOSES several ticks beyond the flag's own boundary, not merely when price touches or barely crosses it.
candidates.pseudocode: isConfirmedDownsideBreakout = close[0] < open[0] && close[0] <= flagLowPrice - marginTicks * tick
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (breakout-confirmation test feeding a continuation entry)

complexity.reason: a bare comparison of the close against a stored flag-boundary price plus a fixed tick margin

notes: Same shape as CloseAbovePriorSwingHighByMargin (V02-18) / CloseAboveEmaByMargin (V02-17), applied to a flag's own boundary instead of a swing high or the EMA.

candidates.name: FadeFailedLowSetupWhenTrendSuspectedReversing
candidates.quote: traders will place a limit order to buy at the low or one to three ticks below the low of that short signal bar, expecting a small higher low to form instead of a profitable low 1 short... In the Emini, they usually can risk as few as four ticks.
candidates.description: When context suggests a bear trend may be reversing to a bull trend, do not take the low-1/low-2 short setups the bear flag still produces; instead place a limit order to buy at (or a few ticks below) that short signal bar's own low, expecting it to fail and form a small higher low instead. Mirrors to fading high-1/high-2 shorts when a bull trend is suspected to be reversing down.
candidates.book_order_type: limit buy at or a few ticks below the low-1/low-2 short signal bar's low

complexity.reason: gated on 'the trend is suspected to be reversing', a discretionary judgment with no stated bar-level test in this passage

notes: Brooks: 'The only time that a low 1 short is reliable is in the spike phase of a strong bear trend, and never after a reversal pattern' - i.e. this fade is meant to be used specifically once a reversal pattern (like a wedge bottom) has already fired.

candidates.name: DoubleFailedBreakoutPredictsOppositeTrend
candidates.quote: Bar 3 was also a second failed attempt to break out to a new high of the day. When the market tries to do something twice and fails both times, it usually trends in the opposite direction.
candidates.description: When price makes two separate attempts to break out to a new extreme in the same direction and both fail (fail to hold beyond the extreme and close back inside the prior range), expect the market to trend in the opposite direction.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context classification feeding a countertrend entry)

complexity.reason: needs the extreme to be a confirmed swing pivot and a count of failed-breakout attempts against it across a bar window

notes: Likely duplicate of DoubleFailedTestTriesOpposite (VP1-04) mined from the Part I introduction chapter; dedup pass should merge.

candidates.name: ClimaxVolumeSpike
candidates.quote: Bar 1 had 93,000 contracts, which was about 10 times the average volume of quiet bars over the past couple of days, and was therefore supportive of a spike and climax type of reversal up.
candidates.description: A trend bar's volume at or above K times the recent average volume of quiet bars supports classifying it as a climax bar (a sign of exhaustion likely to be followed by at least a scalp-sized reversal).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (signal-bar quality test feeding a climax/reversal classification)

complexity.reason: a window average of volume compared against the current bar's volume

notes: The 10x figure is repeated twice in this chapter (93,000 and 105,000 contracts, both '~10 times' the quiet-bar average) - consistent enough to trust as Brooks's own rule of thumb.
'Average volume of quiet bars' (excluding other climax/trend bars) is a stricter definition than a plain N-bar average; avgVolume(lookback) here is a simplification, flagged in this note.

candidates.name: ExceptionallyStrongMomentumOnlyTradeWithTrend
candidates.quote: When the bullish momentum is exceptionally strong, it is better to look only for buy setups and not shorts until after there has been some significant sign of strength by the bears.
candidates.description: When trend momentum is exceptionally strong, suppress all countertrend (reversal) entries until the opposing side shows a significant, explicit sign of strength - a final-flag reversal signal alone is not enough.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'exceptionally strong momentum' and 'significant sign of strength' are both undefined
suppressShortEntries = momentumScore[0] >= exceptionallyStrongThreshold && !bearsShowedSignificantStrength;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (global suppression filter on countertrend entries)

complexity.reason: both 'exceptionally strong momentum' and 'significant sign of strength' have no stated bar-level test; a design decision is needed for both

notes: Likely duplicate of NoCountertrendInStrongTrendWithoutBreak (V02-35); dedup pass should compare.

candidates.name: SpikeTailSignalsOneMorePushThenScalpPullback
candidates.quote: if there is a strong bear spike with four consecutive large bear trend bars mostly closing near their lows, many traders will short around the close of each bar. If the next bar has a big tail on the bottom or a bull body, the bear trend is intact, but traders believe that a pullback is imminent... Aggressive bulls know this and will buy at the bottom of the spike.
candidates.description: During a strong trend-bar spike, once a bar forms with a prominent tail against the spike direction or an outright opposite-colored body, treat it as a signal that the spike has one more small push left before a pullback: take a final with-trend scalp at that bar's close, then look to fade the very next push for a countertrend scalp back toward that bar's own extreme.
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the market/close for the final with-trend scalp; buy at or below the spike's own low for the countertrend fade

complexity.reason: cross-bar state (consecutive large trend bar count) plus single-bar tail/body arithmetic; no pivot detection required since the spike's own extreme is a running max/min, not a confirmed swing

notes: This is effectively a micro (one-bar) final flag defined by shape (tail/opposite body) rather than by the multi-bar overlap test in V07-01.

rejected.quote: How can I be sure? Because if they did, the market would go down, but since it is going up, they must be buying. At some point, everyone realized that this bear flag was never going to break to the downside.
rejected.reason: circular narrative reasoning about unobservable institutional intent, not a bar-level test

rejected.quote: As the market fell, the absence of pullbacks triggered momentum sell programs, contributing to the strength of the sell-off.
rejected.reason: claims about other market participants' algorithmic order flow, not data this engine has access to beyond the resulting OHLCV, which is already captured by the price/momentum candidates above

chapter_summary: Chapter 7 generalizes every trend-ending pause into a 'final flag' candidate (V07-01): a mostly-horizontal, high-overlap pullback after a mature trend, tradable the same way whether or not it turns out to be the actual last one. It works through the failure cascade in detail - a failed final flag becomes a breakout pullback in the original trend (V07-03), and a failed breakout pullback sets up a second entry back in the original reversal direction (V07-04) - plus a micro (1-2 bar) version driven by failed micro-trend-line breaks (V07-02) or spike tail bars (V07-16). Several candidates give concrete numbers Brooks rarely provides elsewhere: a 50%-overlap threshold for two-sided trading (V07-01), a ~10x-average-volume climax-volume test repeated twice in the chapter (V07-14), and a 10-20 bar trend-extreme retest window after a climax-spike final flag (V07-06). A cluster of candidates (V07-08 trend-line-break requirement, V07-13 double-failed-breakout, V07-15 exceptionally-strong-momentum filter) are near-duplicates of primitives already mined in the Part I introduction chapter (VP1-01, VP1-04, V02-35) and should be merged by the dedup pass. V07-05 (shrinking double flags), V07-07 (trading-range midpoint magnet), V07-09 (very-long-trend caveat), and V07-12 (fading failed low1/low2 setups in a suspected reversal) are kept research/low-confidence since Brooks gives no numeric test for 'smaller', 'in a trading range', or 'suspected reversing'. The back half of the chapter (Figures 7.1-7.11, pages 224-244) is entirely worked chart examples with bar numbers; no additional general rules beyond restatements of the above were found there.
